summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)).
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court denied State-agent immunity to the CA/N investigator, who never made the home visit required by Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-34-.05(1)(b), and to the ongoing worker, who ignored her supervisor's binding written instructions, but granted immunity to the two supervisors whose duties involved judgment.
key_cases.relevance: It shows precisely which regulatory omissions defeat immunity when a child dies under agency supervision.
key_cases.quote: because Watson has not submitted substantial evidence indicating that she complied with subsection (b), Watson has not demonstrated that she is entitled to State-agent immunity

key_cases.case_name: Brakefield v. Alabama Department of Human Resources
key_cases.holding: The Court declined to overrule Mitchell v. Davis and held that foster parents are protected by parental immunity from simple-negligence claims by a foster child, so the negligence claims arising from the child's drowning were barred, while the wantonness claims could proceed.
key_cases.relevance: Only wanton, not negligent, conduct by foster parents is actionable when a child dies under agency supervision.
key_cases.quote: negligence claims against the Spurgeons are barred by the doctrine of parental immunity

key_cases.holding: The Court held that DHR employees sued over a foster placement in which the child was harmed were entitled to State-agent immunity because the plaintiffs produced no substantial evidence that the workers violated detailed mandatory rules - including DHR's relative-placement policy and foster-home minimum standards - or acted willfully or in bad faith.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the plaintiff's evidentiary burden after harm to a child under agency supervision.
key_cases.quote: We agree with the petitioners and hold that they satisfied their burden of establishing that they were entitled to State-agent immunity based on Ex parte Cranman.

key_cases.holding: The Court restated the rule governing State-agent immunity into five categories of protected conduct subject to two exceptions - conduct that federal or state law requires otherwise, and conduct that is willful, malicious, fraudulent, in bad faith, beyond authority or under a mistaken interpretation of law - and held that university physicians treating a student fell within no protected category and so were not immune.
key_cases.relevance: This is the source of the standard every Alabama child-fatality suit against DHR staff is measured by, including Ex parte Watson and Ex parte McClintock.
key_cases.quote: when the State agent acts willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith, beyond his or her authority, or under a mistaken interpretation of the law

key_cases.holding: The Court adopted the Cranman plurality's restated State-agent immunity test as the holding of the Court and denied the employees' mandamus petition because the families might still prove that an employee failed to discharge duties pursuant to detailed rules such as a checklist or acted willfully, maliciously, fraudulently, in bad faith, beyond authority or under a mistaken interpretation of law.
key_cases.relevance: It is the decision that supplies the checklist exception later used to deny immunity to the workers in Gowens and Ex parte Watson after children were killed or injured.
key_cases.quote: We today adopt this new test suggested in Cranman.

key_cases.holding: After six foster children died in a foster-home fire the Court held that parental immunity extends in qualified form to foster parents and to the DHR commissioner, county director and case supervisor standing in loco parentis, barring simple-negligence but not wantonness claims, and that the county DHR itself is a State agency absolutely immune under Article I, section 14.
key_cases.relevance: It draws the negligence/wantonness line that determines whether any damages remedy survives a child's death under agency supervision.
key_cases.quote: we hold that foster parents may assert the defense of parental immunity against claims of simple negligence brought by foster children in their care
